description: Delhi HJS 2026 by Delhi High Court: 27 District Judge Entry Level posts. Applications closed 15 July, prelims exam on 26 July 2026. Syllabus and pattern inside.
content:
## Delhi HJS 2026: what this examination is

The Delhi High Court has notified 27 vacancies for the Delhi Higher Judicial Service (DHJS) 2026, recruiting District Judges at Entry Level for the Delhi judiciary. The 27 posts include 24 existing vacancies and 3 anticipated vacancies. Applications opened on 1 July 2026 and closed on 15 July 2026, with the Preliminary Examination scheduled for 26 July 2026 (11:00 AM to 1:00 PM).

If you're one of the applied candidates preparing for the prelims exam on 26 July, this page covers the exam pattern, syllabus, past cutoff trends, and preparation strategy. If you're planning to apply for the next DHJS cycle (expected mid-2027), this page also covers the eligibility route, competing pathways in Indian higher judiciary, and career progression as a district judge.

The DHJS route is one of the two primary paths into the Indian higher judiciary. The other is the state-level Higher Judicial Service exam (each state runs its own), and both feed into the District Judge cadre.

## Preliminary examination on 26 July 2026: pattern and syllabus

The prelims is a 2-hour objective-type MCQ paper of 150 marks. It's qualifying only, does not count toward final merit. Passing the prelims is the gate to the Mains exam.

**Marks distribution:**

| Section | Approximate marks | Question count (approx) |
|---|---|---|
| General Knowledge | 20 | 20 |
| Current Affairs | 15 | 15 |
| Aptitude and Reasoning | 25 | 25 |
| Constitutional Law | 30 | 30 |
| Civil Law (CPC, Contract, TP) | 25 | 25 |
| Criminal Law (IPC/BNS, CrPC/BNSS, Evidence) | 25 | 25 |
| Judicial Precedents (Landmark cases) | 10 | 10 |

**Negative marking:** One-fourth mark deducted per wrong answer. Unattempted questions carry no penalty.

**Qualifying marks:** Delhi High Court sets the qualifying cutoff after the exam based on candidate performance. Historical cutoffs (past 3 cycles): General 55% to 60%, OBC 50%, SC/ST 45%.

**Last-mile preparation priorities:**

1. Revise Constitutional Law: fundamental rights, DPSPs, judicial review, writ jurisdiction, federal structure. Aim for 25 of 30 marks.
2. Revise CrPC and Evidence Act: procedural provisions and landmark evidentiary rules. Aim for 20 of 25 marks in Criminal Law.
3. Practice reasoning and aptitude with 2 daily mock tests. Aim for 20 of 25 marks.
4. Skim recent Supreme Court and Delhi High Court judgments (past 12 months). Focus on constitutional and criminal law judgments.
5. Solve at least 3 previous years' DHJS prelims papers. Time yourself strictly.

## Main examination pattern

Candidates who clear the Preliminary Examination proceed to Main Examination, held approximately 6 to 8 weeks after prelims result.

**Four papers, each of 200 marks and 3 hours duration. Total 800 marks.**

Paper I: General Legal Knowledge and Judgment Writing. Constitutional Law essay questions, judicial ethics, and one full judgment writing exercise on a given fact pattern.

Paper II: Civil Law. Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), Contract Act, Transfer of Property Act, Specific Relief Act. Long-form questions with case-law analysis.

Paper III: Criminal Law. Indian Penal Code / Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, Code of Criminal Procedure / Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023, Indian Evidence Act / Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023. Long-form questions with case-law analysis.

Paper IV: Language and Judgment Writing. Legal translation from English to Hindi and vice versa, judgment drafting exercise, and short essay on a legal topic.

Main exam is descriptive and merit-decisive. Aim for 60% aggregate (480 of 800) to have a strong final merit chance.

## Viva-voce interview

Interview stage carries 200 marks. Panel typically comprises the Chief Justice of Delhi High Court or a designated senior judge, plus 2 to 3 other members including judicial officers and legal academics.

Areas of assessment:

- Legal knowledge and reasoning ability
- Judicial temperament and demeanour
- General awareness and current affairs
- Language skills (Hindi and English)
- Career motivation and understanding of judicial service

Preparation involves current affairs mastery for last 12 months, mock interviews with retired judges or senior advocates (Delhi's judicial community is small and networked), and clear articulation of your motivation for judicial service versus continuing legal practice.

## Salary and career progression as District Judge

Delhi HJS is one of the highest-paying entry paths into the Indian judiciary. Starting salary and career trajectory below.

**Starting salary (year 1 to 2):** Pay Level 12, basic Rs. 51,550, total in-hand approximately Rs. 95,000 to Rs. 1,10,000 per month including DA (46%), HRA (24% for Delhi), and other allowances.

**Year 3 to 5 (Additional District Judge):** Basic pay progression through regular increments. Total in-hand approximately Rs. 1,20,000 to Rs. 1,40,000 per month.

**Year 6 to 10 (District Judge with Selection Grade):** Pay Level 13 with basic Rs. 78,800. Total in-hand approximately Rs. 1,50,000 to Rs. 1,80,000 per month.

**Year 11 to 15 (Senior District Judge, Selection Grade):** Pay Level 14 with basic Rs. 1,44,200. Total in-hand approximately Rs. 1,95,000 to Rs. 2,20,000 per month.

**Judicial elevation to High Court (rare, high-merit):** After 10 to 15 years as a District Judge with distinguished performance, elevation to the Delhi High Court bench is possible via the collegium recommendation process. High Court judges get Pay Level 17 with basic Rs. 2,25,000.

**Non-financial benefits:** Official residence, government vehicle with driver, chamber and staff, full family medical coverage, education allowance for children up to graduation, and a defined-benefit pension after retirement (age 60 for District Judges, 62 for High Court judges).

## Two eligibility routes: in-service versus advocate

DHJS 2026 has two eligibility routes with different competitive dynamics.

**Route 1: In-service judicial officers.** Currently serving Delhi Judicial Service (Munsif or Metropolitan Magistrate) officers with minimum 7 years of continuous service can apply. This route is a career fast-track for existing lower-court judges who don't want to wait for the internal promotion queue.

**Route 2: Advocates.** Advocates enrolled with any State Bar Council with minimum 7 years of continuous practice can apply. This is the primary route for practising lawyers who want to shift into the judiciary.

Historical selection ratio: Approximately 60% of DHJS selections have come from Route 2 (advocates), 40% from Route 1 (in-service). The written exam is designed to test judicial thinking rather than practising skills, which tends to level the field between the two routes.

## Preparation resources for future cycles

For candidates planning to apply for DHJS 2027 (expected notification mid-2027):

**Books:**

- Constitution of India by MP Jain (Comprehensive)
- CPC by CK Takwani (Practical)
- Criminal Procedure by RV Kelkar
- Evidence Act by Ratanlal and Dhirajlal
- Landmark Judgments of Supreme Court by Universal Law Publishing

**Online resources:**

- SCC Online for case law
- LiveLaw and Bar and Bench for current judicial developments
- Delhi High Court's own website for previous years' DHJS question papers

**Coaching options:** Delhi has several judiciary-focused coaching institutes (Rahul's IAS, Rankers Judiciary, JudiciaryGold). Fees range Rs. 60,000 to Rs. 1,50,000 for a 6 to 8 month full course.

**Realistic preparation timeline:** For an advocate with 7+ years of practice starting fresh preparation, 12 to 18 months of dedicated study is typical. In-service judicial officers can prepare in 8 to 12 months due to their existing familiarity with procedural law.

## Judiciary as a career vs private practice

Two questions candidates often ask before deciding to prepare for DHJS.

**Question 1: Should I leave private practice for the judiciary?**

Financial trade-off: An advocate with 7+ years of practice earning Rs. 2 lakh to Rs. 5 lakh per month at a good firm or in independent practice takes a temporary pay cut moving to DHJS (starting Rs. 1 lakh). By year 5 to 7, DHJS salary catches up. By year 10 with Selection Grade, DHJS often exceeds practice income. Beyond financials: job security, defined pension, prestige of judicial office, and predictable work-life balance are the non-monetary benefits that draw many advocates.

**Question 2: What's the acceptance chance for a first-time applicant?**

Historical selection ratio: 27 posts against approximately 8,000 to 12,000 applications means about 1 in 300 to 1 in 400 applicants get selected. First-time applicants have a lower success rate than repeat applicants. Realistically expect 2 to 3 attempts before final selection, with each attempt building on cumulative preparation.

If you're weighing DHJS 2026 outcomes for planning your next 12 months, treat the Q4 FY 2026-27 mains result as the decision point. If shortlisted for mains, focus 100% on interview preparation from October 2026. If not shortlisted, use the Q1 FY 2027-28 window to plan DHJS 2027 or state HJS applications.

## DHJS vs other higher judicial services

If DHJS 2026 is your primary target but you're also considering state HJS routes, this comparison helps map competing options.

| Judicial service | Vacancies (typical) | Starting basic | Notification cycle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delhi HJS | 20 to 30 | Rs. 51,550 | Annual, Q2 |
| Uttar Pradesh HJS | 100 to 150 | Rs. 51,550 | Every 2 to 3 years |
| Maharashtra HJS | 40 to 60 | Rs. 51,550 | Annual, Q1 |
| Karnataka HJS | 30 to 50 | Rs. 51,550 | Annual, Q3 |
| Tamil Nadu HJS | 20 to 40 | Rs. 51,550 | Every 2 years |
| West Bengal HJS | 30 to 60 | Rs. 51,550 | Every 2 to 3 years |
| Rajasthan HJS | 20 to 40 | Rs. 51,550 | Annual, Q2 |

Starting basic pay is identical across states (Pay Level 12 in the 7th CPC pay matrix). What varies is DA, HRA (city classification), and non-financial perks (government housing quality, court infrastructure, judicial support staff). Delhi HJS is generally considered the most prestigious given the concentration of Supreme Court, Delhi High Court, and central-government litigation in the capital.

For a first-time DHJS applicant not selected in the 2026 cycle, applying for state HJS the same year is a strong parallel strategy. State HJS syllabi have significant overlap with DHJS on core legal papers, and preparation done for DHJS transfers cleanly to state HJS with minor state-specific additions.

## Documents to keep ready

For candidates who applied for DHJS 2026 and are approaching the prelims exam on 26 July, keep these documents ready at the exam centre.

- Original admit card printout (colour, on A4 sheet)
- Valid photo ID (Aadhaar, PAN, Voter ID, Passport, or Driving Licence)
- Two recent passport-size photographs (same as uploaded during application)
- Blue or black ballpoint pen
- Analog wristwatch (mobile phones and smartwatches not allowed inside exam hall)

Documents to keep ready for later stages if you clear prelims:

- Original degree certificates (10th, 12th, LLB, LLM if applicable)
- Bar Council enrollment certificate
- Practice certificate from your High Court or Bar Council confirming 7+ years of practice
- Character certificate from a Bar Council member or Judicial Officer
- Recent income tax returns for last 3 years (for advocate route)
- Service record for in-service applicants

Missing documents at the interview stage lead to disqualification even if written exam scores are strong. Prepare all originals plus 3 photocopies at least 30 days before the mains result.
qualification: Bachelor of Laws (LLB) degree from a recognised university, either 3-year LLB or 5-year integrated LLB. LLM or NET/SET is not mandatory but advantageous for merit ranking in the interview stage.

content:
## UPSC CDS 2 2026: exam on 13 September

UPSC Combined Defence Services Examination II 2026 is recruiting 451 officer cadets across four academies, and the written examination is on 13 September 2026. UPSC notified it on 20 May 2026 and the application window opened the same day, closing in June 2026.

CDS is the graduate route into the armed forces as an officer. Where the NDA takes candidates straight after Class 12, CDS takes graduates, which makes it the examination most people mean when they ask how to become an army officer after college.

One scheduling note worth flagging early: the NDA and NA II 2026 written examination falls on the same date, 13 September 2026. Candidates in the narrow age band where both are open cannot sit both, so that choice has to be made in advance rather than discovered on the day.

## The four academies, and why the choice matters

This examination fills four very different destinations, and candidates routinely apply without understanding the difference.

| Academy | Location | Leads to | Commission type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Indian Military Academy (IMA) | Dehradun | Army officer | Permanent Commission |
| Indian Naval Academy (INA) | Ezhimala | Navy officer | Permanent Commission |
| Air Force Academy (AFA) | Dundigal, Hyderabad | Air Force officer | Permanent Commission |
| Officers Training Academy (OTA) | Chennai | Army officer, men and women | Short Service Commission |

The distinction that matters most in that table is the last column, and it deserves more than a passing mention because it shapes an entire career.

## Permanent Commission versus Short Service Commission

A Permanent Commission through IMA, INA or AFA is a full career. You serve until the retirement age for your rank, you are eligible for pension, and promotion runs the full length of the officer ladder.

A Short Service Commission through OTA is an initial engagement of a defined term, extendable in stages, with the option to apply for a Permanent Commission during service subject to vacancies and selection. Officers who are not granted one leave at the end of their tenure with terminal benefits rather than a full career pension.

That is not a reason to avoid OTA. It is the only route in this examination open to women, it has a wider age band, and the training period is shorter. But a candidate should choose it knowing what it is, rather than discovering the distinction after selection.

The practical guidance: if you are eligible for IMA, INA or AFA and want a full military career, preference those. Take OTA if you specifically want the shorter commitment, if you are a woman candidate, or if you are outside the age or subject requirements for the permanent-commission academies.

## Written exam pattern: two different exams

CDS is really two examinations sharing one application, and confusing them costs preparation time.

For IMA, INA and AFA, there are three papers.

| Paper | Marks | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| English | 100 | 2 hours |
| General Knowledge | 100 | 2 hours |
| Elementary Mathematics | 100 | 2 hours |
| Written total | 300 | |

For OTA, there are two.

| Paper | Marks | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| English | 100 | 2 hours |
| General Knowledge | 100 | 2 hours |
| Written total | 200 | |

OTA candidates do not sit the Elementary Mathematics paper at all. If you are applying only for OTA, the entire mathematics syllabus is irrelevant to you, which is a substantial saving in preparation time that many candidates fail to take.

Add the SSB interview and the totals become:

| Route | Written | SSB | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| IMA, INA, AFA | 300 | 300 | 600 |
| OTA | 200 | 200 | 400 |

Note that the SSB carries the same weight as the entire written examination in both routes. Clearing the written paper gets you to the interview; it does not get you selected.

Negative marking applies at one third of the marks assigned to a question for each wrong answer. With that penalty, blind guessing is close to break-even and adds variance, so answer where you can eliminate at least one option and leave the rest.

## Syllabus

English tests comprehension, vocabulary, grammar and usage at graduate level, through reading passages, sentence improvement, error spotting, synonyms and antonyms, and ordering of words and sentences.

General Knowledge covers current affairs, Indian history with emphasis on the freedom movement, geography, Indian polity and the Constitution, economics, general science covering physics, chemistry and biology, and defence-related awareness. The defence portion rewards specific study: ranks and insignia, military exercises, indigenous defence programmes, and recent acquisitions appear regularly and are ignored by candidates preparing from a general competitive syllabus.

Elementary Mathematics, for IMA, INA and AFA only, sits at Class 10 level and covers arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry, geometry, mensuration and statistics. It is the most scoring of the three papers for anyone comfortable with school mathematics, since the questions are direct and the syllabus is closed.

## Eligibility

Requirements differ by academy, and applying to one you do not qualify for wastes the attempt.

| Academy | Education | Age band (approximate) | Who can apply |
|---|---|---|---|
| IMA | Graduate in any discipline | About 19 to 24 | Unmarried men |
| INA | Engineering degree | About 19 to 24 | Unmarried men |
| AFA | Graduate with Physics and Mathematics at 10+2 level, or an engineering degree | About 20 to 24 | Unmarried men |
| OTA (men) | Graduate in any discipline | About 19 to 25 | Men |
| OTA (women) | Graduate in any discipline | About 19 to 25 | Women |

The exact birth-date windows are fixed in each notification and shift every cycle, so confirm them against the advertisement rather than relying on the approximate bands above.

Two conditions catch people out. INA requires an engineering degree specifically, so an arts or commerce graduate cannot apply there however strong the application. AFA requires Physics and Mathematics at the 10+2 level even for graduates in other subjects, which excludes candidates who dropped those subjects after Class 10.

Final-year students may apply, subject to producing proof of passing by the date specified in the notification.

## The SSB interview

The Services Selection Board interview runs over five days and carries the same weight as the entire written examination.

Day one is screening, with an officer intelligence rating test and a picture perception and discussion test, after which a substantial share of candidates are sent home the same day. Day two is the psychology round, covering the thematic apperception test, word association test, situation reaction test and self description. Days three and four cover the group testing officer tasks, including group discussion, group planning, progressive group tasks and command tasks, alongside the personal interview. Day five is the conference at which the board takes its decision.

The board assesses officer-like qualities rather than knowledge: reasoning, decision-making under pressure, initiative, responsibility, and the ability to work within and lead a group. Preparation for it is unlike exam study, and it rewards mock SSB sessions, honest self-assessment, and genuine familiarity with your own background, since the interview draws heavily on what you say about yourself.

A medical examination follows selection, and the standards are strict, particularly on vision for the Air Force route.

## Training after selection

Selection leads to training rather than a posting, and the length differs by academy.

Cadets selected for IMA undergo about 18 months of training at Dehradun before being commissioned as Lieutenants in the Army. INA cadets train at Ezhimala, AFA cadets at Dundigal near Hyderabad, and the duration varies by branch and specialisation, with flying training for the Air Force running longer than ground branches.

OTA cadets at Chennai complete a shorter course, around 49 weeks, reflecting the Short Service Commission structure.

Training is residential, physically demanding and academically structured, covering military tactics, weapons handling, drill, physical conditioning, map reading, and service-specific technical subjects. Cadets receive a stipend during the pre-commission training year, and full officer pay begins on commissioning rather than on joining the academy, which is a distinction worth understanding before you plan finances around selection.

## Comparing CDS with the other officer routes

Graduates aiming at a uniformed officer career usually have several options, and they differ in more than the syllabus.

| Route | Entry after | Selection | Leads to |
|---|---|---|---|
| CDS | Graduation | Written plus SSB | Army, Navy or Air Force officer |
| NDA | Class 12 | Written plus SSB | Army, Navy or Air Force officer |
| CAPF Assistant Commandant | Graduation | Written, physical, interview | Central armed police forces |
| AFCAT | Graduation | Written plus AFSB | Air Force officer, flying and ground duty |
| Territorial Army | Graduation | Written plus interview | Part-time commissioned service |

CDS and NDA both go through the SSB and both lead to the same three services, differing in entry point. [CAPF Assistant Commandant](/sarkari-naukri/upsc-capf-ac-2026) leads into the paramilitary rather than the armed forces and carries a heavier physical component. AFCAT is the Air Force's own examination and is worth sitting alongside CDS if the Air Force is the target, since it offers a second route to the same destination.

A candidate serious about a commission should generally sit more than one of these in a cycle. The SSB preparation is common to CDS, NDA and AFCAT, so the marginal cost of an extra application is small and the additional chance is real. The one constraint to check is the calendar: where two written examinations fall on the same date, as CDS II and NDA II do this cycle on 13 September 2026, the choice has to be made at application stage rather than left open.

## Salary and career

Officers commissioned through CDS enter at Level 10 of the pay matrix with a basic pay of Rs 56,100, plus Military Service Pay of Rs 15,500 a month and dearness allowance, which brings in-hand pay at commissioning to roughly Rs 1,00,000 to Rs 1,25,000 depending on posting and allowances.

Progression runs through the officer ranks: Lieutenant at Level 10, Captain at Level 10B, Major at Level 11, Lieutenant Colonel at Level 12A, Colonel at Level 13, Brigadier at Level 13A and Major General at Level 14, with Military Service Pay applying throughout. Promotion to Captain and Major is time-bound; above Lieutenant Colonel it becomes selective.

Beyond pay, the package includes subsidised accommodation, ration entitlements, medical cover for the officer and dependants including ECHS after retirement, group insurance, leave travel concession and pension for permanent commission officers.

## Preparing in the remaining weeks

With the written examination on 13 September, there are about six weeks from the time of writing.

Work out first which papers you actually need. An OTA-only candidate preparing Elementary Mathematics is wasting a third of their effort.

Prioritise General Knowledge, since it is the paper with the widest range and the one where a systematic approach separates candidates most. Cover current affairs of the past year and give specific attention to defence awareness, which is high-yield and neglected.

Treat Elementary Mathematics as the scoring paper if you are sitting it. The syllabus is closed and at Class 10 level, so practice converts directly into marks in a way that General Knowledge does not.

For English, read and practise rather than study grammar theory. Comprehension and usage questions reward familiarity, and a candidate who reads a newspaper daily and works one practice set a day will outperform one who studies grammar rules in isolation.

Work past papers under the two-hour clock for each paper, and train the marking decision: with a one third penalty, know your own accuracy rate on questions where you have eliminated one option.

Begin SSB preparation in parallel rather than after the result. It carries half the total marks, it cannot be crammed, and the gap between the written result and the interview call is not long enough to build officer-like qualities from scratch.

## How to apply in the next cycle

Applications are filed on the UPSC portal at upsconline.nic.in.

1. Complete the One Time Registration if you have not already, since it is reused across UPSC examinations.
2. Open the CDS application when the notification appears and select your academy preferences in order, checking the education and age conditions for each before selecting it.
3. Fill personal and educational details exactly as on your certificates.
4. Choose your examination centre early, since centres fill on a first-apply basis.
5. Upload photograph and signature in the specified format.
6. Pay the fee of Rs 200. SC, ST and female candidates are exempt.
7. Submit and save the registration number and application PDF.

UPSC runs CDS twice a year, as CDS I and CDS II, so a missed window is a six-month wait rather than a year.

## Frequently asked questions

**When is the UPSC CDS 2 2026 exam?**
The written examination is on 13 September 2026. UPSC notified the examination on 20 May 2026 for 451 vacancies and the application window opened the same day, closing in June 2026. Note that the NDA and NA II 2026 written examination falls on the same date, so candidates eligible for both must choose between them.

**How many vacancies are in CDS 2 2026?**
There are 451 vacancies across the Indian Military Academy, Indian Naval Academy, Air Force Academy and Officers Training Academy for both men and women. The academy-wise split is set out in the notification, and IMA and OTA typically account for the largest shares.

**What is the difference between IMA, INA, AFA and OTA in CDS?**
IMA at Dehradun leads to an Army officer commission, INA at Ezhimala to the Navy, and AFA at Hyderabad to the Air Force, and all three grant a Permanent Commission. OTA at Chennai leads to an Army officer commission under a Short Service Commission and is the only route in this examination open to women. The commission type is the most consequential difference: a Permanent Commission is a full career with pension, while a Short Service Commission is a defined engagement with the option to apply for a permanent one during service.

**Is the CDS exam pattern different for OTA?**
Yes. IMA, INA and AFA candidates sit three papers, English, General Knowledge and Elementary Mathematics, at 100 marks each for a written total of 300. OTA candidates sit only English and General Knowledge for a written total of 200 and do not take the mathematics paper at all. Each paper is two hours. An OTA-only candidate preparing mathematics is wasting a third of their effort.

**What are the total marks in CDS?**
For IMA, INA and AFA the written examination is 300 marks and the SSB interview 300, for a total of 600. For OTA the written examination is 200 and the SSB 200, for a total of 400. In both routes the SSB carries the same weight as the entire written paper, so clearing the written examination gets you to the interview rather than to selection.

**Is there negative marking in CDS?**
Yes, one third of the marks assigned to a question is deducted for each wrong answer. With that penalty, blind guessing is close to break-even and adds variance, so the sensible approach is to answer where you can eliminate at least one option and leave alone the questions where you have no basis.

**What is the age limit for CDS 2 2026?**
The bands vary by academy, running approximately 19 to 24 years for IMA and INA, about 20 to 24 for AFA, and about 19 to 25 for OTA for both men and women. Exact birth-date windows are fixed in each notification and shift every cycle, so confirm them against the advertisement rather than an approximate band.

**Can women apply for CDS?**
Yes, through the Officers Training Academy route, which leads to a Short Service Commission in the Army. The IMA, INA and AFA routes in this examination are for unmarried male candidates. Women candidates sit the two-paper OTA written examination of English and General Knowledge, followed by the SSB interview.

**What qualification is needed for CDS?**
IMA and OTA require a graduate degree in any discipline. INA requires an engineering degree specifically, so arts and commerce graduates cannot apply there. AFA requires a graduate degree with Physics and Mathematics studied at the 10+2 level, or an engineering degree. Final-year students may apply subject to producing proof of passing by the date specified in the notification.

**What is the salary of an officer selected through CDS?**
Commissioning is at Level 10 of the pay matrix with a basic pay of Rs 56,100, plus Military Service Pay of Rs 15,500 a month and dearness allowance, giving in-hand pay of roughly Rs 1,00,000 to Rs 1,25,000 depending on posting and allowances. Subsidised accommodation, rations, medical cover including ECHS after retirement, group insurance and pension for permanent commission officers apply on top.

**How is CDS different from NDA?**
NDA is the officer entry straight after Class 12, at 16.5 to 19.5 years, with a written examination of 900 marks plus a 900-mark SSB. CDS is the graduate route, at roughly 19 to 25 years depending on academy, with a written examination of 300 or 200 marks plus an SSB of matching weight. Both use the five-day SSB interview. For the 2026 cycle both written examinations fall on 13 September, so they cannot both be attempted.

**How many times a year is CDS conducted?**
Twice, as CDS I and CDS II, so a missed application window means roughly a six-month wait rather than a full year. That cadence also means a candidate within the age band typically gets several attempts, unlike recruitments held once annually.

content:
## Indian Navy SSC Officer 2026 to 275 officer posts, apply by 27 July

Indian Navy has opened applications for the June 2027 (AT 27) Short Service Commission Officer course. Total 275 tentative vacancies across 12 branches. Applications are live at joinindiannavy.gov.in and close on **27 July 2026**.

You're eligible if you hold a BE/B.Tech (or the specific PG qualification for Education, Logistics, and Naval Armament branches), are unmarried, and were born between the dates specified for your branch. Selection is through SSB Interview and medical, with training at Indian Naval Academy, Ezhimala from June 2027.

There is no application fee, and both men and women can apply for most branches.

---

## Important dates

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Notification released | 25 June 2026 |
| **Online application opens** | **25 June 2026** |
| **Last date to apply** | **27 July 2026** |
| SSB interview call-up | Announced individually after shortlisting |
| Training commences | June 2027 (INA Ezhimala) |

Applications close at midnight on 27 July. No extensions have been announced in recent SSC Officer cycles, so treat this deadline as final.

---

## Vacancy breakdown: 275 posts across 12 branches

The Navy has published a tentative branch-wise split. Vacancies may adjust based on training slot availability at INA.

| Branch | Posts | Open to |
|---|---|---|
| Executive (GS(X) / Hydro) | 90 (incl. 10 Hydro) | Men & Women |
| Electrical (GS) | 40 (8 + 32) | Men (8) / Men & Women (32) |
| Pilot | 25 | Men & Women |
| Engineering (GS) | 24 | Men & Women |
| Naval Air Operations Officer | 18 | Men & Women |
| Naval Constructor | 18 | Men & Women |
| Air Traffic Controller | 15 | Men & Women |
| Naval Armament Inspectorate | 14 | Men & Women |
| Education | 13 (5 + 8) | Men & Women |
| Logistics | 10 | Men & Women |
| Submarine Tech Electrical | 8 | Men only |
| Submarine Tech Engineering | Vacancies to be notified | Men & Women |

Executive branch has the largest share at 90 posts. Pilot and NAOO are the most competitive because of the strict medical and higher-education standards, plus a hard cap on women intake per branch.

---

## Who can apply?

### Age limits (date-of-birth ranges)

| Branch | Born between |
|---|---|
| Most branches | 2 July 2002 to 1 January 2008 |
| Pilot / NAOO / Observer | 2 July 2003 to 1 July 2008 |
| Air Traffic Controller | 2 July 2002 to 1 July 2006 |
| Education | 2 July 2002 to 1 July 2006 |

Your date of birth on your 10th class certificate is what the Navy accepts. Any mismatch means rejection at document verification.

### Educational qualifications by branch

**Executive, Pilot, NAOO, Air Traffic Controller**
BE/B.Tech in any discipline, minimum 60 percent aggregate. Pilot, NAOO, and ATC candidates also need 60 percent in Class 10 and 12, and 60 percent in English marks in either 10th or 12th.

**Engineering (GS)**
BE/B.Tech with 60 percent in Marine, Instrumentation, Production, Aerospace, Mechanical, Metallurgy, Mechatronics, or Aeronautical Engineering.

**Electrical (GS) and Submarine Tech Electrical**
BE/B.Tech with 60 percent in Electrical, Electronics, or related disciplines.

**Naval Constructor**
BE/B.Tech with 60 percent in Mechanical, Civil, Aeronautical, Marine, Naval Architecture, or Metallurgy.

**Naval Armament Inspectorate**
BE/B.Tech with 60 percent in Mechanical, Aeronautical, Electrical, Electronics, IT, Chemical, Metallurgy, and related streams; or a PG degree in Electronics/Physics. Class 10/12 aggregate 60 percent with 60 percent English.

**Education Branch**
MSc/MA in Mathematics, Physics, History, Oceanography, and related subjects; or BE/B.Tech (Mechanical, Electrical, Electronics); or ME/M.Tech. Class 10/12: 60 percent with 60 percent English.

**Logistics**
BE/B.Tech First Class; or MBA First Class; or B.Sc/B.Com/B.Sc(IT) First Class plus PG Diploma in Finance, Logistics, or Supply Chain; or MCA/M.Sc(IT) First Class.

Final-year students may apply, but you must have your provisional or final degree in hand before training starts in June 2027.

### Physical standards

Height, weight, vision, and chest measurements follow Navy medical standards, which differ slightly by branch. Corrective eye surgery (LASIK) is permitted for some branches under conditions listed in the official notification. Read your branch section carefully before applying, a medical rejection late in the process is a wasted year.

---

## What is the salary of a Navy SSC Officer?

Your gross monthly pay at commissioning as Sub Lieutenant is approximately **₹1,20,000**. The break-up:

| Component | Approximate Amount |
|---|---|
| Basic Pay (Level 10, 7th CPC) | ₹56,100+ |
| Military Service Pay | ₹15,500 |
| Dearness Allowance | On basic + MSP |
| Kit Maintenance / other allowances | Variable |

Post-training, if you're commissioned as a Pilot, Naval Air Operations Officer, or Submariner, you get an additional **flying / submarine allowance of ₹31,250 per month**. Officers posted in field areas or hard areas get further allowances.

Non-monetary benefits are substantial:

- Rent-free furnished accommodation (or HRA if quarters unavailable)
- Comprehensive medical care through Armed Forces Medical Services for you and dependents
- Subsidised meals at officers messes
- Canteen (CSD) privileges, significant savings on white goods and staples
- Group insurance cover of ₹75+ lakh
- Leave Travel Concession, free travel to home town every year
- Family pension after commissioning

SSC tenure is 10 years, extendable to 14 years. Progression from Sub Lt → Lt → Lt Cdr → Cdr is time-scale, so promotions don't depend on interviews.

---

## How to apply: step by step

1. Open **joinindiannavy.gov.in** and click on **Officer Entry**
2. Select the **June 2027 (AT 27)** course notification
3. Register with a valid email ID and mobile number. Both should remain active until your SSB call-up, the Navy sends everything to email
4. Fill in personal, educational, and branch preference details. You may list up to two branches
5. Upload photograph, signature, and left thumb impression in the sizes specified on the form
6. Preview the application, fix any errors, and submit
7. Print the acknowledgement page and keep it safe

No corrections are allowed after submission. Take an hour on Sunday, sit down with your certificates, and fill it in one clean sitting.

---

## Selection process

There is no written exam. The Navy screens applications and calls shortlisted candidates directly for SSB Interview.

### Application shortlisting

The Navy applies a branch-wise cut-off based on your normalised percentage across 10th, 12th, and graduation marks. Cut-offs are announced only after applications close. Historical cut-offs for Executive have hovered near 70 percent; Pilot and NAOO have been closer to 75 percent.

### SSB Interview (5 days)

Reporting centres: Bangalore, Bhopal, Coimbatore, Visakhapatnam, or Kolkata. The Navy assigns your centre.

**Day 1: Screening**
Officer Intelligence Rating tests and Picture Perception & Discussion Test. Around 50 percent of candidates get eliminated on Day 1.

**Day 2: Psychology tests**
Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), Word Association Test (WAT), Situation Reaction Test (SRT), and Self-Description Test (SDT). You write under time pressure, practise TAT stories in advance.

**Day 3 and 4: Group tasks and interview**
Group Discussion, Group Planning Exercise, Progressive Group Task, Half Group Task, Command Task, Individual Obstacles, Snake Race, Final Group Task, Lecturette. Plus a one-on-one Personal Interview with the IO. The Navy is checking leadership, decision-making under pressure, and how you behave in a group.

**Day 5: Conference**
All assessors meet and finalise the recommendation. Results are declared the same day. Recommended candidates move to medicals; non-recommended candidates go home.

### Medical examination

Recommended candidates go through a detailed medical at the nearest Military Hospital, usually over three to five days. Pilots and Submariners have the strictest standards. Common medical rejections are eyesight below the branch cut-off, high or low blood pressure, and undeclared past surgeries.

### Merit list and joining

Final merit combines SSB marks and medical fitness. Provisional selection letters and joining instructions for INA Ezhimala go out roughly two to three months before the training start date in June 2027.

---

## Should you apply?

If you're a BE/B.Tech student or graduate, unmarried, and under the branch age limit, apply. There is no fee, and even if you don't make it, an SSB call-up is invaluable interview practice for future attempts (CDS, AFCAT, other SSC cycles).

**Why the Navy appeals:**

- Officer rank from day one, unlike JCO or PBOR entries
- ₹1.2 lakh gross at 22 or 23 years old is competitive with tier-1 private companies
- Free medical, quarters, canteen access, and pension add real value on top of pay
- SSC gives you 10 to 14 years of service, long enough to build a career, short enough to shift to civilian life afterward
- Postings across coastal cities and ships, you actually see the country

**Points to weigh:**

- Selection is genuinely hard. Recommendation rates from SSB rarely cross 5 percent
- Postings can be at sea for months at a stretch, not ideal if you value routine
- Medical standards are strict; even one bad marker like colour vision deficiency can disqualify you from Pilot or ATC
- SSC officers don't get a pension unless they complete 20+ years, though gratuity and severance are paid

---

## Frequently asked questions

**When does the Indian Navy SSC Officer 2026 application close?**
27 July 2026. Applications submitted after midnight of this date will not be accepted.

**What is the age limit for Navy SSC Officer 2026?**
Most branches require date of birth between 2 July 2002 and 1 January 2008. Pilot/NAOO/Observer needs DOB between 2 July 2003 and 1 July 2008. ATC and Education need DOB between 2 July 2002 and 1 July 2006.

**What is the salary of a Sub Lieutenant in the Indian Navy?**
Approximately ₹1,20,000 per month gross at commissioning, including Basic Pay (₹56,100 minimum at Level 10 of 7th CPC), Military Service Pay, and Dearness Allowance. Pilot / NAOO / Submarine officers get an additional ₹31,250 per month post-training.

**Is there an application fee for Navy SSC Officer?**
No. There is no application fee for Indian Navy SSC Officer entries.

**Can women apply for Navy SSC Officer 2026?**
Yes. Women can apply for 11 of the 12 branches. Only Submarine Tech Electrical is restricted to men. Some branches have a hard cap on women intake per cycle.

**Is there a written exam for Navy SSC Officer?**
No. The Navy screens applications against branch cut-offs and calls shortlisted candidates directly for SSB Interview. Selection is SSB Interview + Medical only.

**Where is the training for Navy SSC Officer conducted?**
Indian Naval Academy (INA), Ezhimala, Kerala. Training for the AT 27 course starts in June 2027.

**Can final-year students apply?**
Yes. You may apply while in your final year, but you must complete your degree and produce the certificate before training commences in June 2027.

---

## Quick links

- **Apply online**: [joinindiannavy.gov.in](https://www.joinindiannavy.gov.in)
- **Notifications page**: [joinindiannavy.gov.in/notifications](https://www.joinindiannavy.gov.in/en/page/notifications.html)
- **Indian Navy official**: [indiannavy.nic.in](https://www.indiannavy.nic.in)

Pilot, NAOO, and ATC candidates additionally need 60 percent in Class 10 and 12, plus 60 percent English marks. Logistics: BE/B.Tech First Class, or MBA First Class, or B.Sc/B.Com/B.Sc(IT) First Class plus PG Diploma in Finance/Logistics/Supply Chain, or MCA/M.Sc(IT) First Class. Naval Armament Inspectorate: BE/B.Tech with 60 percent in Mechanical, Aeronautical, Electrical, Electronics, IT, Chemical, Metallurgy, or related streams; or PG degree in Electronics/Physics. content:
The West Bengal Public Service Commission issued Advertisement No. 13/2024 on 25 April 2026 for the Miscellaneous Services Recruitment Examination. Applications ran from 30 April to 20 May 2026 and closed at 3:00 PM on the final day.

One thing to be clear about immediately: the Commission has not announced how many posts this recruitment will fill. Any specific vacancy figure you have seen for this cycle, including one that appeared on this page previously, is unsourced.

## Where this recruitment stands

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Advertisement | No. 13/2024, dated 25 April 2026 |
| Application window | 30 April to 20 May 2026, closed |
| Vacancy total | Not announced |
| Preliminary exam | Not announced |
| Stages | Preliminary, Final written, Personality Test |
| Portal | psc.wb.gov.in |

WBPSC publishes vacancy details for this examination at a later stage rather than in the initial advertisement, and the number moves as participating departments confirm requirements. That is normal practice for this recruitment and not a sign of anything being withheld.

If you saw a figure of 900 posts on this page previously, it was not sourced and has been removed rather than replaced with a different guess.

## What Miscellaneous Services actually covers

This examination fills Group B and Group C posts across West Bengal government departments. The name is accurate: the posts are genuinely miscellaneous, spanning administrative, revenue and inspection roles rather than a single cadre.

Posts recruited through this route have historically included Revenue Inspector, Sub-Inspector of Schools, Assistant Superintendent in various directorates, Block Welfare Officer and comparable departmental positions. The exact list for a given cycle is set out in the advertisement and in the vacancy notification that follows.

The common thread is that these are executive positions with real administrative responsibility at district and block level, below the West Bengal Civil Service grades but well above clerical entry. For a graduate who wants to work in West Bengal government administration without competing in the far narrower WBCS field, this is the main route.

## The three stages

The Preliminary Examination is objective and functions as a screening filter. Its marks do not carry into the final merit list. WBPSC calls forward a multiple of the eventual vacancy count, which is one reason the vacancy announcement matters even though it comes later.

The Final Examination is conventional, meaning descriptive written papers rather than multiple choice. This is the transition that ends most attempts. Candidates who prepared by drilling objective questions arrive at a descriptive paper without having written structured answers under time, and the gap shows immediately.

The Personality Test is the interview stage, conducted by the Commission after the written result.

Final merit is built from the Final Examination and the Personality Test together. Nothing from the preliminary stage carries forward.

## Why the descriptive stage decides everything

The shift from objective prelims to conventional finals is the single most important structural feature of this examination, and it is the one candidates prepare for least.

An objective paper rewards recognition. You see an option and identify whether it is right. A conventional paper rewards production. You have to generate a structured, relevant answer in your own words, inside a time limit, legibly, several times over.

Those are different skills, and the second is slower to build. A candidate can raise an objective score substantially in a few weeks of practice. Building the ability to write clear, well-organised answers at speed takes months.

The practical implication is that answer writing should start well before the preliminary result, not after it. Candidates who wait for the result have a compressed window to acquire the skill that actually determines their rank, while candidates who began earlier arrive at the finals already fluent.

Write in the language you intend to use in the examination and stay in it, rather than switching between Bengali and English during preparation.

## The preliminary paper in more detail

The preliminary examination is a single objective paper covering general studies at graduate level, with a substantial West Bengal component alongside the national material.

The scope runs across Indian history with emphasis on the freedom movement, geography of India and West Bengal, Indian polity and the constitution, the economy at national and state level, general science and its everyday applications, environment and ecology, reasoning and mental ability, and current affairs at both national and state level.

Two features of the paper are worth planning around. It is broad rather than deep, so a candidate who has covered everything at a moderate level generally outperforms one who has covered half the syllabus thoroughly. And the West Bengal portion is disproportionately valuable, because it is where candidate performance actually varies. Everyone has read the standard national material. Far fewer have worked systematically through West Bengal history, geography and administration.

Negative marking applies, so the usual discipline holds: an unattempted question costs nothing while a low-confidence guess costs marks. Confirm the exact deduction for this cycle in the advertisement rather than assuming it from another examination.

Because the paper is a filter and its marks are discarded, the target is comfortable qualification rather than a high score. Time spent pushing a prelims score well past the cutoff is time not spent on the descriptive stage that actually decides your rank.

## Building West Bengal specific knowledge

Since the state portion is where the examination separates candidates, it is worth setting out what that material actually covers and how to approach it.

West Bengal history spans the Bengal Renaissance, the partition of Bengal, the state's role in the freedom movement, and post-independence political development. This is not a small body of material and it rewards systematic reading rather than skimming a compilation.

Geography covers the state's physical divisions, river systems including the Ganga-Hooghly network, soils, climate, agriculture, mineral resources and industrial geography. Questions frequently turn on specific detail rather than broad understanding.

Polity and administration covers the structure of the state government, panchayati raj in West Bengal, municipal administration, and the departments this recruitment actually places you into. Knowing the administrative structure is doubly useful, because it is examinable and it is the environment you will work in.

Economy covers the state's agricultural profile, industrial position, major schemes run by the state government, and current budget priorities. State schemes appear regularly and change often, which is why this belongs in your current affairs routine rather than in a one-time reading.

Board publications and state government sources are the primary material. Coaching compilations are useful for revision and should not be the base layer, since errors propagate between them and a compilation is only as good as whoever assembled it.

## Answer writing for the conventional stage

Given how much rests on the descriptive papers, it is worth being concrete about what good answer writing looks like.

Address the question actually asked. Descriptive papers use directive words that mean different things: describe, explain, discuss, examine and critically assess each demand a different treatment, and answering all of them by writing everything you know about the topic is the most common way marks are lost.

Structure visibly. An introduction that frames the answer, a body organised into identifiable parts, and a conclusion that returns to the question. An examiner reading many scripts rewards a structure they can follow.

Respect the word limit and finish. An incomplete answer scores as incomplete no matter how strong its opening paragraphs were, and running long on early questions guarantees running short on later ones.

Write legibly. This sounds trivial and it is not. Handwriting that is hard to read costs marks in practice regardless of content quality, and it degrades under time pressure unless you have practised at speed.

Practise with a timer from the beginning. Writing a good answer with unlimited time proves little. The examination tests production under constraint, and the constraint has to be part of the practice.

Get answers evaluated where you can. Self-assessment plateaus quickly because the errors you cannot see are precisely the ones you need identified.

## Eligibility

The academic requirement is a graduate degree from a recognised university.

The age band runs from 20 to 39 years against the reference date stated in the advertisement, with relaxation for reserved categories under West Bengal rules. That upper limit of 39 is considerably more generous than most central recruitments allow, and it makes this examination a viable route for candidates who have aged out of other options.

Knowledge of Bengali is generally required, consistent with administration in West Bengal being conducted in the state language. The specific wording, including any exemption for candidates from particular districts, is set out in the advertisement and should be checked against your own position.

Confirm every condition against Advertisement No. 13/2024 rather than a summary. WBPSC varies eligibility between cycles and the advertisement is what binds.

## What to prepare while the exam date is pending

WBPSC had not announced the preliminary examination date at the time of writing, which makes this a preparation phase rather than a countdown.

Put weight on West Bengal specific material. State history, geography, economy, polity, administrative structure, schemes and current affairs form a substantial part of the paper, and this is the portion with the thinnest available resources. National general studies material is abundant and every candidate has it. The state portion is where the field separates.

Run current affairs daily and keep state-level notes separate from national ones. National compilations do not cover West Bengal schemes, appointments, budget announcements or district developments, and those appear in the paper.

Begin answer writing now at low volume, two answers a week, for the reasons set out above. This feels premature with no date announced and it is the highest-return thing available.

Work through previous years' papers to learn the level and the phrasing rather than to memorise questions.

Check psc.wb.gov.in on a fixed weekly schedule. The Commission publishes and does not individually notify.

## How this compares with WBCS

Candidates in West Bengal weigh these two against each other, and the comparison is worth making explicitly.

| | WBPSC Miscellaneous | WBCS |
|---|---|---|
| Post level | Group B and C executive | Group A and B, including WBCS Executive |
| Competition | Heavy | Considerably heavier |
| Upper age | 39 | Lower, varies by group |
| Stages | Prelims, conventional finals, interview | Prelims, mains, personality test |
| Career ceiling | Departmental progression | District administration and above |

WBCS is the more prestigious route and the harder one. Miscellaneous Services fills a large number of executive posts with meaningful responsibility, and the wider age band makes it accessible to candidates for whom WBCS is closed.

The preparation overlaps substantially. General studies, West Bengal specific content and answer writing serve both, which is why many candidates sit both examinations in the same period rather than choosing between them.

## Preparing for a recruitment of unknown size

It is unusual to prepare for an examination without knowing how many posts it will fill, and it changes the calculation in ways worth thinking through.

The competition ratio is unknown until the vacancy notification appears. A recruitment that turns out to fill several hundred posts is a very different proposition from one that fills a few dozen, and candidates naturally want that number before committing months of preparation.

The practical answer is that it should not change what you do. The preparation for this examination is the same regardless of the eventual count: general studies breadth, West Bengal depth, and descriptive answer writing. None of that becomes more or less worth doing because the number turns out higher or lower.

What the unknown does affect is how you plan around it. Do not build a strategy that depends on the recruitment being large. Sit other examinations you are eligible for in the same period rather than treating this as your single route, because the preparation transfers and the calendar rarely collides badly.

And treat the eventual announcement as information rather than as a verdict. A smaller-than-hoped count does not waste the preparation, which remains valid for the next cycle and for parallel examinations, and this recruitment runs periodically rather than once.

The one thing to avoid is planning around a figure someone published without a source. That is worse than planning around no figure at all, because it produces false confidence in either direction.

## After selection: what the work involves

Candidates focus heavily on clearing the examination and rarely on what the posts actually involve day to day, which is worth correcting before you commit years to the route.

These are executive positions in state government departments, and the work is administration in the real sense: implementing schemes, maintaining records, conducting inspections, handling public interaction, and applying rules to individual cases. A Revenue Inspector deals with land records and revenue matters. A Sub-Inspector of Schools deals with educational administration within a defined area. The specifics vary enormously by department.

Postings are within West Bengal and typically at district or block level, particularly early in service. Candidates expecting a Kolkata posting from the outset are usually disappointed, and a willingness to work in district administration is close to a prerequisite for being satisfied in the role.

Progression runs through departmental promotion, and the pace depends on the department and on vacancies arising. It is steady rather than fast.

The genuine attractions are security, a defined pay structure with pension provision, and authority over matters that affect people directly at the local level. The trade is that the work is procedural, the geography is fixed to one state, and the pace of advancement is slower than a comparable private sector track.

Weigh that honestly before the preparation rather than after the posting.

## Common mistakes

Relying on an unsourced vacancy figure. WBPSC has not announced a total for this cycle, and planning around a number someone published without a source is planning around nothing.

Preparing only with objective practice. The final examination is conventional and descriptive, and objective drilling does not build the skill it tests.

Postponing answer writing until after the prelims result. The window is too short to acquire the skill then.

Reading only national current affairs. The West Bengal portion is where the paper is decided and national compilations do not cover it.

Waiting for the Commission to notify you of the examination date. WBPSC publishes on its website and does not send individual notifications.

Switching preparation language midway. Decide on Bengali or English early and build fluency in one.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many vacancies are there in WBPSC Miscellaneous Services 2026?**

The Commission has not announced a total. WBPSC publishes vacancy details for this examination at a later stage rather than in the initial advertisement, and the figure moves as departments confirm requirements. Any specific number circulating for this cycle is unsourced.

**Can I still apply?**

No. Applications ran from 30 April to 20 May 2026 and closed at 3:00 PM on the final day. There is no late route.

**When is the WBPSC Miscellaneous preliminary exam?**

Not announced as of 18 August 2026. WBPSC will publish the date on psc.wb.gov.in. Any date quoted elsewhere is an estimate rather than an announcement.

**What is the selection process?**

Three stages: a Preliminary Examination that is objective and screens the field, a Final Examination that is conventional and descriptive, and a Personality Test. Preliminary marks do not carry into the final merit list, which is built from the Final Examination and the Personality Test together.

**What is the age limit?**

20 to 39 years against the reference date in the advertisement, with relaxation for reserved categories under West Bengal rules. The upper limit of 39 is more generous than most central recruitments, which makes this a viable route for candidates who have aged out of other options.

**What qualification is needed?**

A graduate degree from a recognised university. Knowledge of Bengali is generally required, consistent with state administration being conducted in the state language, and the specific wording including any exemptions is set out in the advertisement.

**What posts does this examination fill?**

Group B and Group C executive posts across West Bengal government departments. Posts recruited through this route have historically included Revenue Inspector, Sub-Inspector of Schools, Assistant Superintendent in various directorates and Block Welfare Officer. The exact list for a cycle is in the advertisement and the vacancy notification.

**Is the final examination objective or descriptive?**

Conventional and descriptive, not multiple choice. This is the most important structural feature of the examination and the one candidates prepare for least, because objective drilling builds recognition while a descriptive paper requires you to produce structured answers under time.

**How does this compare with WBCS?**

WBCS recruits to higher grades including WBCS Executive and is considerably more competitive. Miscellaneous Services fills Group B and C executive posts with real administrative responsibility, and its upper age limit of 39 makes it accessible to candidates for whom WBCS is closed. The preparation overlaps substantially, so many candidates sit both.

**When will the vacancy count be announced?**

WBPSC publishes it later in the process rather than with the advertisement. Watch psc.wb.gov.in. Until then, treat the recruitment as one of unknown size rather than assuming a figure from a previous cycle or from an aggregator.

**Does WBPSC publish previous years' cutoffs?**

The Commission publishes cutoff marks after a cycle concludes, varying by category. They move with paper difficulty, applicant volume and the eventual vacancy count, so a historical figure is orientation for your mock scores rather than a target to aim at. With this cycle's vacancy total still unannounced, historical cutoffs are a particularly weak guide.

**Can I write the examination in Bengali?**

The conventional papers may generally be written in Bengali or English, and candidates are not disadvantaged by choosing Bengali given that state administration is conducted in it. Confirm the language provisions in Advertisement No. 13/2024. Whichever you choose, practise consistently in that language rather than switching, because fluency in written examination conditions is language-specific.

## Official sources

- West Bengal Public Service Commission: https://psc.wb.gov.in
- Advertisement No. 13/2024, which is the authority on eligibility wording, age reference date, the post list and the examination scheme

Where anything on this page conflicts with the advertisement or a subsequent Commission notice, the Commission is correct.

content:
## BHEL Engineer Trainee 2026: what to expect

Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) is expected to release the Engineer Trainee 2026 recruitment notification in July 2026, based on BHEL's annual recruitment cycle and prior year patterns. The 2026 cycle is expected to include approximately 150 vacancies for Engineer Trainee positions across four core disciplines: Mechanical Engineering, Electrical Engineering, Civil Engineering, and Metallurgical Engineering.

BHEL is India's largest engineering and manufacturing enterprise in the power sector, with 16 manufacturing units and 6 corporate offices across India. Engineer Trainee is the gateway entry-level position for fresh B.E./B.Tech graduates via GATE 2026 score. Starting CTC approximately Rs. 12 to Rs. 14 lakh per annum with full CPSE benefits.

If you're a B.E./B.Tech candidate in ME/EE/CE/Metallurgy with a valid GATE 2026 score, this recruitment is one of the most competitive PSU entry points annually. This page tracks the expected 2026 notification, covers eligibility, selection process, salary structure, career progression, and how to prepare for the personal interview stage that decides final merit.

## What BHEL Engineer Trainees do

Engineer Trainees join BHEL as E-2 grade officers with a 1-year structured training programme covering the full breadth of BHEL's business verticals.

**Training verticals:**

1. Power Sector (thermal, hydro, nuclear, renewables). Design, manufacturing, and commissioning of power plants.
2. Industry Sector (transportation, transmission, oil and gas, defence). Products and services for industrial customers.
3. International Business (overseas projects, EPC contracts in Africa, Middle East, Southeast Asia).
4. R and D and Innovation (electric mobility, hydrogen technology, energy storage).

**Post-training deployment.** Confirmed BHEL Engineers work across BHEL's 16 manufacturing units (Bhopal, Hyderabad, Jhansi, Tiruchirappalli, Ramachandrapuram, Haridwar, Bengaluru, Ranipet, Rudrapur, and others), 6 corporate offices, and various customer sites and overseas project locations.

Career progression: Engineer Trainee to Engineer (post-training) at E-3 grade in year 2. Senior Engineer at E-4 in years 4 to 5. Deputy Manager E-5 in years 6 to 8. Manager E-6 in years 10 to 12. Progression continues to Senior General Manager and Chairman level for high-performers over 25 to 30 years.

## Eligibility in detail

Four qualifying disciplines with GATE 2026 discipline-match requirement.

**Discipline 1: Mechanical Engineering.** B.E./B.Tech in Mechanical Engineering, Production Engineering, Manufacturing Engineering, Industrial Engineering, or Automobile Engineering. Valid GATE 2026 score in ME paper. Typical BHEL cutoff for General category: GATE score 550+ (out of 1000).

**Discipline 2: Electrical Engineering.** B.E./B.Tech in Electrical Engineering, Electrical and Electronics Engineering, or Power Systems Engineering. Valid GATE 2026 score in EE paper. Typical cutoff: 500+.

**Discipline 3: Civil Engineering.** B.E./B.Tech in Civil Engineering, Structural Engineering, or Construction Engineering. Valid GATE 2026 score in CE paper. Typical cutoff: 480+.

**Discipline 4: Metallurgical Engineering.** B.E./B.Tech in Metallurgy, Materials Engineering, or Metallurgical and Materials Engineering. Valid GATE 2026 score in MT paper. Typical cutoff: 450+.

**Age limit:** Not more than 27 years as on the notification date. Age relaxation: SC/ST 5 years, OBC 3 years, PwD 10 years, ex-servicemen per Government of India norms.

**Minimum marks:** 60% aggregate for General/OBC/EWS. 55% for SC/ST/PwD. Marks below cutoff disqualify the application regardless of GATE score.

## GATE 2026 score and merit calculation

BHEL Engineer Trainee 2026 uses GATE 2026 score directly for both shortlisting and final merit. Understanding this is critical for candidates deciding whether their GATE score is competitive enough to apply.

**Shortlist ratio:** 1:5 (5 candidates called for interview per vacancy). For 150 vacancies, approximately 750 candidates will be shortlisted based on GATE scores. Discipline-wise shortlist ratios may vary based on vacancy distribution.

**Final merit formula:** GATE score contributes 75% weightage, Interview score contributes 25%. So a candidate with GATE 600 and Interview 70/100 has:
- GATE contribution: 600 x 0.75 = 450
- Interview contribution: 70 x 0.25 = 17.5
- Total merit: 467.5

**Realistic GATE cutoffs for 2026 selection (based on prior cycles):**

| Discipline | General | OBC | SC/ST | EWS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanical (ME) | 550+ | 520+ | 460+ | 530+ |
| Electrical (EE) | 500+ | 470+ | 420+ | 490+ |
| Civil (CE) | 480+ | 450+ | 400+ | 470+ |
| Metallurgy (MT) | 450+ | 420+ | 380+ | 440+ |

If your GATE 2026 score is close to or above the applicable cutoff, applying is worthwhile. Below the cutoff, interview-stage compensation is unlikely to make up the gap.

## Personal Interview and Group Discussion preparation

The 25% interview weightage means a strong interview can move a candidate 10 to 15 rank positions in the final merit list. Preparation matters.

**Technical questions (60% of interview):**

- Core discipline knowledge from GATE syllabus (heat transfer, thermodynamics, power system analysis, structural mechanics, phase diagrams, and process metallurgy depending on discipline)
- Applied engineering questions specific to BHEL's business (steam turbine design, HVDC transmission, cement plant machinery, welding of heavy structures)
- Industry current affairs (energy transition, India's renewable capacity addition, BHEL's product portfolio and recent contracts)

**Communication and general awareness (25% of interview):**

- Current affairs of last 12 months (India and international)
- BHEL's history, product line, financial performance, and strategic direction
- Basic government policies related to power sector, MSME sector, and Make in India

**Behavioural questions (15% of interview):**

- Career motivation for public sector engineering
- Handling of academic project failures or team conflicts
- Approach to relocation and long-hours industrial work

**Group Discussion topics** (typical):

- India's transition to renewable energy vs continued reliance on coal-based power
- Role of PSUs in India's economic growth story
- Make in India and BHEL's contribution
- Cost vs quality trade-offs in Indian manufacturing

Prepare with mock interviews at least 3 times before the actual interview. GATE-based coaching institutes (Made Easy, Gate Academy, IES Master) offer BHEL-specific interview coaching for Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 30,000.

## Salary progression and career path

Detailed salary and career progression at BHEL.

**Year 1 (Engineer Trainee, E-2):** Basic pay Rs. 40,000. Total CTC Rs. 12 to Rs. 14 lakh per annum. Includes DA, HRA, LTC, medical, and other allowances.

**Year 2 to 4 (Engineer, E-3):** Basic pay progression to Rs. 60,000. Total CTC Rs. 16 to Rs. 18 lakh per annum.

**Year 5 to 7 (Senior Engineer, E-4):** Basic pay Rs. 70,000 to Rs. 80,000. Total CTC Rs. 20 to Rs. 24 lakh per annum.

**Year 8 to 12 (Deputy Manager, E-5):** Basic pay Rs. 90,000 to Rs. 1,00,000. Total CTC Rs. 25 to Rs. 30 lakh per annum.

**Year 13 to 18 (Manager, E-6):** Basic pay Rs. 1,10,000 to Rs. 1,30,000. Total CTC Rs. 32 to Rs. 40 lakh per annum.

**Year 19 onwards (Senior Manager and beyond):** Continued progression through Senior General Manager, Executive Director, and CMD levels for high performers. Basic pay Rs. 1,50,000+ with executive-tier benefits.

Non-financial benefits: Government housing at BHEL townships (subject to availability). Company transport for daily commute. Full family medical coverage including senior parents. Education allowance for children up to graduation. LTC every 2 years for domestic destinations. Post-retirement medical benefits.

## Why BHEL Engineer Trainee vs other PSU entries

BHEL Engineer Trainee has three distinct advantages over other PSU engineering entries via GATE.

**1. Broader technology exposure.** BHEL's business spans thermal, hydro, nuclear, renewables, transmission, transportation, oil and gas, and defence. Engineers rotate across verticals during training and can specialise later. NTPC, PGCIL, and IOCL offer narrower technology exposure.

**2. Faster career progression to executive tier.** BHEL's promotion cycle to Senior General Manager (equivalent to Joint Secretary in central government) takes 20 to 22 years for high-performers, compared to 25 to 28 years at IOCL or GAIL.

**3. Manufacturing depth for hard-skill development.** BHEL is one of India's few remaining large-scale heavy-industry manufacturers. Engineers who complete 5 to 7 years at BHEL are highly sought by private-sector employers like Siemens, GE, Larsen and Toubro Power, and Tata Power for their manufacturing and heavy-industry expertise.

If you're weighing BHEL against NTPC, PGCIL, or IOCL for the July 2026 GATE-based cycle, BHEL's manufacturing depth and technology breadth make it the strongest choice for candidates prioritising long-term skill development over immediate high-tech exposure.

## BHEL manufacturing units and posting preferences

BHEL operates 16 manufacturing units, 6 corporate offices, and various regional installations across India. Understanding the posting geography helps applicants plan.

**Major manufacturing units:**

- Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh (transformers, motors, large power equipment)
- Hyderabad, Telangana (turbines, generators, boilers)
- Trichy, Tamil Nadu (boilers, seamless tubes, valves)
- Ranipet, Tamil Nadu (industrial boilers, capacitors)
- Ramachandrapuram, Andhra Pradesh (heavy castings and forgings)
- Bhopal Additional, Madhya Pradesh (motors and small equipment)
- Haridwar, Uttarakhand (hydro turbines, thermal power equipment)
- Bengaluru, Karnataka (electronics, control systems, R and D)
- Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh (transformers, locomotives)
- Rudrapur, Uttarakhand (compressors, misc equipment)

**Posting policy for Engineer Trainees:** First posting is usually not at the applicant's preferred location. Expect posting to one of the smaller regional units for the first 3 to 5 years. Metro-city and preferred-region postings become available on internal transfer after 5 years of confirmed service, subject to vacancy and performance.

**Township living:** Most major BHEL units have engineer townships with government-subsidised housing, schools, hospitals, and recreation facilities. Rent-free official housing for 2 to 3 years after confirmation is standard.

## Documents to keep ready for the interview

Candidates who clear the shortlist based on GATE 2026 score must produce these originals plus 2 copies at the interview.

- GATE 2026 scorecard (original and printout)
- B.E./B.Tech degree certificate and mark sheets (all semesters)
- 10th class mark sheet and certificate
- 12th class mark sheet and certificate
- Category certificate (if applicable) in Central Government format
- Income and asset certificate for EWS (if applicable)
- Disability certificate for PwD (if applicable)
- Ex-servicemen discharge certificate (if applicable)
- Aadhaar card and PAN card
- 4 recent passport-size photographs
- Character certificate from college
- Any internship or work experience certificates
